title: Beginner who wants to make a game using AI - what's the "best" stack for an AI-only workflow?
author: kavakravata
selftext:
Hey!

My lifelong dream has been to make my own game. I have a vision, an idle game - for a start. I want to come up with all features and level design etc, but I don't want to code, nor to design UI, levels, models etc.

I'm technical but don't have much time, I want to avoid clicking through software's to build stuff, I want to outsource all to the AI.

The game should be accessible on Steam once finished, and playable offline.

What's my best bet in terms of stack?

Much obliged!

comments.author: YoshiBanana3000
comments.body:
If you are a beginner, my best advice is not to start with your dream projet... Start easy, with a real simple app/game.   
Build the prototype  
Learn how to build an architecture, how to test, how to debug, how to build assets  
Go to production  
Learn all the marketing  
Learn how to maintain a game over time

Restart with a little more ambitous project.  
Learn more.

And then, you will be way more mature to make your dream comes true.

replies.author: PairOfPixelsGS
replies.body:
Best is subjective, because it depends on each one's experience, but we are kinda on the same page. I'm also a dad, and I have a full time job so AI opened a lot of doors for me to start creating my game. So here is my personal experience:  
\- Dev: 

 \--Unity. I use Unity because of C#, which I have 20 years of experience, so for me it was an obvious choice to ramp up. But it's a great tool, and they are releasing Unity AI, their own agent to create assets. So It's worth to take a look (it's in beta currently)

 \-- Claude Code: great AI for coding. It solves complex issues and can implement your features as you go. Unity AI is worth a try too.

\- Art: 

  \-- Midjourney to create 2D art. Magnific to scale image when needed (I have 2D background images). I use the seed feature so you can create an art style and apply to each image you create, which means you have consistent images.

  \-- Gemini to fine tune art and correct imperfections, remove / isolate elements

  \-- Meshy to create 3D model from 2D image generated on Midjourney

  \-- AccuRig to rig 3D models (Not AI tool but it's worth mentioning)

  One important note. Even using all AI tools, there are some manual process that are easier if you are familiar with the engine you are working on.

That's it in a nutshell. Good luck!

replies.author: PairOfPixelsGS
replies.body: In my case I don't need to connect MCP, but Unity has one if you want to use Claude inside Unity directly. I use in Visual Studio Code with Claude extension installed. One of the Claude "flavors" when you have a subscription is Claude Code, so you can open the game folder in Claude, and it will know your code and you can prompt directly in your code base. If you feel that MCP is more practical, go for it, but for me this workflow works very well.

comments.author: rekansebangku
comments.body:
From my point of view, I haven't seen a fully AI built and designed Steam game that’s actually good yet. Or I could be wrong, since there's already an ocean of AI games on Steam now. But to stand out, I think you have to do at least some of the boring/hard stuff yourself, because relying solely on AI will just produce more AI slop.

For a starting point, though, I’d recommend using Claude Code or Cursor with MCP alongside a game engine, and Nano Banana/GPT for 2D assets, or Meshy for 3D stuff. I don't know about animation, though. not sure which model is best for that.

comments.author: Nostradamivre
comments.body:
First of all: you can do it, but...! (Assuming you're making a full game, not a browser game — those aren't bad, just simpler and quicker to make in general.)

Is this your first time ever? Do you have any experience in coding or game design? What's the scope? These aren't dismissive questions — they'll define the duration of the project. You said you're "technical" — at what? Because in game design you can be technical on so many levels it's ridiculous.

Here's what I've seen a lot and experienced firsthand:

**The coding part**

If you have base knowledge in coding (any language), you'll work faster just by taking your steps in the right order. With Claude you can bypass this at the beginning, but after N+ iterations things are gonna crack. Knowing a bit of code logic makes the process easier, I promise. (E.g.: in HTML you're not gonna put the core game engine in the header — everyone who's done a bit of web knows this with their eyes closed, but if you've never tried it, how could you?) Claude is very good at this as long as you define a protocol and workflow that work for you (it's astonishing in JavaScript). Even if you've never coded before, you can work around these with good protocol and workflow — all done in Claude by "vibe" coding.

**Assets**

Then the hard part: making a game is about mechanics, logic, level design, menu design, etc. You said you want to "avoid clicking through software to build stuff" — OK, but you still have to vibe it into something. If you don't want to open Blender, you still need to describe what you want, and it's exhausting if you've never done 3D modeling or graphic design. [Meshy.ai](http://Meshy.ai) is good for this, but dang, you can lose yourself in it. A 30-something box in the asset stores will get you further in no time — just don't asset-flip (everyone notices, don't be a fool).

**Architecture**

After some time you'll have something, and the big question appears. Monolithic? Sure, if your game is around 14K lines and revolves around 2 or 3 mechanics — no special modes, no campaign, no challenge mode. But assuming your idea is bigger, you'll have to choose: which language, which platform (Claude and Unity work nicely, Godot is my go-to, and for JavaScript there's Babylon, crazy stable for 2.5D and 3D), or the big ones like Unreal. They all have good and bad points depending on your goal.

This is where it gets really complicated: cross-referencing things in the engine. Being absolutely sure of what to change and where is a game changer in gamedev. You can scan it with Claude or any AI to find what's going on — but can you spot a hallucination? Something created by a previous prompt that breaks your game at any point? That's the thing about vibe coding without knowing basic code. Good workflow and protocol prevent most of it.

Archive your work and iterations — it saves a lot of time, and updating your project in Claude helps a lot. When you hit 18K/20K lines, divide your work: engine and mechanics first, then UI, then UX. And if you're still monolithic at that point — time to switch.

Last thing on languages: today you can use pretty much whichever you want, BUT hear me — not all code is copy/paste from one to another, so depending on what you're doing, choose carefully.

**Shipping**

The rest is your own limits and motivation when things go south. Testing is hard — way harder than people assume, because you play your own game for hours and the spark goes away. Offline games are a go-to: security protocols are hard for online (anti-cheat and everything). Steam leaderboards are easy to integrate and very safe. Do a decent job and you'll pass Steam quality control (some ass games are out there, nothing surprises me anymore), and after that the rest is history.

comments.author: teamharder
comments.body:
ThreeJS at least for your first couple of prototypes. Unity if you want to use human made assets to improve the look. Build fast, fail fast, learn fast.

Personally my "stack" is Claude Fable or Opus on the Claude Desktop. My game-dev skill is an orchestrator with 30+ specialized sub-agents. That connects to Unity via MCP. I watch the Unity store, Humble Bundle, and Itch.io for highly discounted 3d assets. I use Ludo.ai to create 2d assets and animations. Suno to create music. Claude used FFMPEG for the trailer.

comments.author: MunchyCerealGuy
comments.body:
Posting for anyone who finds it later:

Former indie-game dev and AI power user here. I believe that AI is going to radically change the traditional game development process. In its end state, AI-centred game dev will be less of an incremental, tool-by-tool pipeline and more a workflow where you start from a self-contained artefact you can see and play from the start

I'm focused on inventing/discovering this newer approach rather than finding ways to speed up each stage of assembly that comes from a pre-AI workflow of game dev

Good news for you specifically: an idle game is one of the friendliest genres for an AI-first workflow since the progression system is relatively linear

The tool I've been building for this is Chatforce (chatforce.com). You describe your game by generating concept art with AI image models and explaining the features in plain English; once the art looks right, it builds a playable version that's a direct match to the concept. The whole point is maximum creative control without clicking through editors or writing code which I myself got frustrated with. Would love for you to try it out!
